Why this session exists

The goal of the day: build the foundations you need to work with AI agents. Four parts, one goal.

An agent works where you work: in a terminal, on files, in a Git repository. When it runs a command, you need to be able to read that command. When it changes a file, you need to see exactly what changed, and undo it if it is wrong. So today you learn the terminal and Git by hand, before any agent touches your files. Then the words for what an agent is made of and where you stand in its loop: the LLM thinks. The harness acts. The human directs and checks. Last, you choose the real engineering or research problem your project will be about for the rest of the semester, and save your first draft of it in Git.

Why these tools? Open source

Closed source: you get the program, not its code (Windows, macOS, Microsoft Word). Open source: the source code is published under a licence that lets anyone read, use, change and share it (Linux, Git, Python, uv). Open source is not "no rules": the licence (MIT, Apache, GPL, …) sets the conditions.

Tool Open source? Why it matters here
Linux (Ubuntu, in WSL on Windows) Yes. The kernel: Linus Torvalds, 1991. Ubuntu is one distribution of it The same kind of terminal on Windows (WSL), on a Mac (a close Unix cousin) and on the servers agents run on. The agent works in it too.
Git Yes. Torvalds again, April 2005, built to manage the Linux kernel's code You can see, compare and undo every change, including an agent's.
Python and uv Yes Free for anyone to install, and uv's lock file rebuilds the same environment on every laptop.
GitHub No: a company's service that hosts Git repositories Git is the tool; GitHub is one place to keep its repositories.

Not everything is: GitHub, Microsoft's build of VS Code and most of the language models we call are not. The course's rule is open-source and free-tier tooling wherever possible.

You can read what a tool does. That is the habit this course asks of you with agents: do not trust it, check it.

Part 1 · The terminal (24 min)

By the end of this part, you can:

  • Move between folders, read files, and download a file.
  • Explain why agents need commands.

Watch 1a · Where you are, and how to read a command (≈8 min, to 10:45)

A terminal is a window where you type commands to interact with your computer. Each command runs from a current directory: the folder you are in now. pwd prints it; cd changes it.

Why learn commands? AI agents can run them too. Understanding commands helps you check what an agent does.

Fig. 2Your home folder as a tree: the home folder ~ holds Documents, treasure (with start and forest inside) and my-project; a marker shows the current directory, the folder you are in now

The tree is a simplified picture. Today's game builds its folder one level deeper, at ~/TA1/treasure.

Reading a command. Five pieces of notation you will meet all day:

Command What it means
cd ~ ~ means your home folder.
cd .. .. means the folder one level above.
cat <file> Replace <file> with a real name, such as README.txt.
echo "hi" > note.txt > writes output to a file and replaces its contents.
echo "more" >> note.txt >> adds output at the end of the file.

Fig. 3One arrow replaces, two arrows append: echo hi with one arrow leaves the file holding only hi; echo more with two arrows adds more as a new last line

Twelve commands, three purposes. They cover today's tasks. You'll learn more as you need them.

Look around Change things Read and get
Where am I, what is here? Make, copy, move, delete. Read, write, download, run.
pwd — Where am I? mkdir <name> — Make a folder cat <file> — Show what is inside
ls — What is in this folder? cp a b — Copy a file echo "hi" > file — Write text into a file
cd <folder> — Go into a folder mv a b — Move or rename a file curl -fLO URL — Download a file
cd .. — Go up one folder rm file — Delete without a recycle bin bash script.sh — Run a script

Predict, then run. Before you run each line, say what it will do. In the HTML version of this handout, the answers are hidden until you click: predict first.

Command What happens
pwd where am I?
ls what is here?
mkdir demo make a folder
cd demo go inside
echo "hello" > hello.txt write a file
cat hello.txt read it
cd .. go up
rm demo/hello.txt delete: no recycle bin!
ls demo empty now

The same nine lines, to run in your own terminal:

pwd
ls
mkdir demo
cd demo
echo "hello" > hello.txt
cat hello.txt
cd ..
rm demo/hello.txt
ls demo

Your turn 1b · The treasure hunt (14 min, 10:45–10:59)

Somewhere in a folder called treasure there is a golden key. Find it using only the terminal.

Step Do this Why
1 Create and enter the TA1 folder: mkdir -p ~/TA1, then cd ~/TA1 Today's games all live in ~/TA1, away from your own files. -p means no error if the folder is already there.
2 Download the setup script: curl -fLO https://technionaifluency.github.io/www/exercises/w01/setup_treasure.sh curl downloads a file. It saves setup_treasure.sh in the folder you are in now, ~/TA1. It prints a small progress table; 100 in the first column means it is done. The download fails? Appendix B.
3 Build the treasure folder: bash ~/TA1/setup_treasure.sh The script creates the game files on your laptop. It ends with Treasure hunt ready! and tells you the next two commands.
4 Go in and read the message: cd ~/TA1/treasure, then cat README.txt The README gives your mission and where to start.
5 Follow the clues. Use ls, cd, cat, mkdir, mv. Each clue file tells you where the next one is. The last one tells you what "finished" means.

Steps 1–4, as on the slide, without its # notes:

mkdir -p ~/TA1
cd ~/TA1
curl -fLO \
https://technionaifluency.github.io/www/exercises/w01/setup_treasure.sh
bash ~/TA1/setup_treasure.sh
cd ~/TA1/treasure
cat README.txt

Hints, one clue at a time. Open one only when you are stuck; each gives a nudge, not the answer. The full route is in Appendix A.

Clue 1 says the next folder is "next to" yours. How do I get there?

"Next to" means: in the same parent folder. Go up one level first. .. means the folder one level above.

Clue 2: three folders, and only one of them is right.

ls shows the three names. Read them: only one has a name about a secret. The other two are dead ends, and their files tell you how to come back.

Clue 3 wants me two levels up. Do I need two commands?

You can, but .. can be chained: ../.. is the folder two levels above. Run pwd afterwards to see where you landed.

Clue 4: two jobs at the end.

One job makes a folder, the other moves a file into it. mkdir and mv from the table above. Make the folder where clue 4 says, not inside the mountain.

Bonus, for fast finishers.

Hidden files start with a dot, and plain ls does not show them. ls -a does.

Done when The key is in done and no longer in mountain. The last clue gives the check:

ls ~/TA1/treasure/done
ls ~/TA1/treasure/mountain

The first prints golden_key.txt. The second no longer lists it.

Things that catch people:

  • On a Mac: zsh: command not found: #, cd: too many arguments, or Usage: bash setup_treasure.sh [--reset]. You typed the slide's # … note too. Type only the part before the #.
  • The download fails (for example curl: (6) Could not resolve host). Use Appendix B: download the file in the browser and copy it into Ubuntu.
  • curl: (56) The requested URL returned error: 404 (older curl: (22)). The address has a typo: compare it with the handout letter by letter, or copy it from the HTML handout, and run the corrected line.
  • No such file or directory. The name or the place is wrong. pwd tells you where you are; ls shows the exact names to type.
  • curl: … no URL specified (added after the session; the exact words depend on your curl version). The curl command is printed on two lines; the \ at the end of the first line means "the command goes on". Press Enter without it and curl runs with no address, then the shell tries to run the address as a command (No such file or directory). Type the whole command on one line, or keep the \ as the last character of the first line.
  • The key is now a file called done (added after the session). mv golden_key.txt done, typed inside mountain before the done folder exists, renames the key instead of moving it. Fix it from inside mountain: mv done golden_key.txt, then cd .., mkdir done, mv mountain/golden_key.txt done/.
  • ls ~/TA1/treasure/done prints a path ending in /done, or mkdir done says File exists. The key was renamed to a file called done in treasure. From ~/TA1/treasure: mv done golden_key.txt, mkdir done, mv golden_key.txt done/.
  • The treasure game already exists. Your progress has been kept. You ran the setup a second time. Nothing is lost: carry on where you were. To start again, bash ~/TA1/setup_treasure.sh --reset (it moves the old game into a hidden backup folder in ~/TA1 and prints its name). Run it from ~/TA1, then cd ~/TA1/treasure again. If you used Appendix B, the script is in your home folder: bash ~/setup_treasure.sh --reset.
  • rm is final. There is no recycle bin in the terminal. Read an rm line twice before you press Enter — and read it three times when an agent asks to run one.

Part 2 · Git: save points (29 min)

By the end of this part, you can:

  • Explain what a save point is, and why we use them.
  • Save versions, switch between existing branches, and undo an edit.

Watch 2a · Save points, baskets and timelines (10 min, 10:59–11:09)

Why Git?

Without Git, versions pile up as files: notes.md, notes_v2.md, notes_final.md, notes_final_REALLY.md, notes_use_this_one.md. Which one is right? What changed? With Git there is one file, and every version is saved, with a label. You can go back.

Git saves versions of your project when you make a commit. You can compare changes and return to an earlier saved version.

How Git saves a version. Three places, two commands:

Fig. 4How Git saves a version: the working folder, where you edit your files; git add puts the change in the basket (staging), the content ready to save; git commit saves it to the history as a snapshot with a label

  • Working folder — where you edit your files.
  • Staging, the basket — the content ready to save.
  • History — snapshots, each with a label.

git add prepares the changes. git commit saves the version.

Branches: separate lines of commits. A branch is a separate timeline of save points. The first one is main. Here, main has three commits, and a second timeline, experiment, starts from the third one to try a risky idea without touching main.

Fig. 5Branches as timelines: main runs through Add first note, Add second note and Add third note; a branch called experiment leaves the third commit for Try a risky idea; HEAD marks where you are

(Source for the note under the figure: git-switch documentation.)

The words of Git.

Term Meaning
Repository A folder that Git watches
Save point (commit) A photo of your files, with a label
Label A short sentence that says what changed
Timeline (branch) A separate line of save points (the first is main)
Basket (staging) The files you chose for the next save point
Untracked, modified New file not saved yet, saved file that changed
HEAD A marker: you are here

All of it on one page:

Fig. 6Git on one page: a repository frame holding the working folder with a modified notes.md, the basket (staging), and the history of labelled save points with HEAD on main and a branch for a risky idea; how a save point is made: edit a file, git add, git commit

Git commands, in plain words. The last column is where you use each one in the Git Quest.

Command Plain words In the quest
git init Create a repository here Part 4, in your project
git status What does Git see right now? Level 1 (and every level)
git log --oneline Show commits on this branch Level 1
git branch Show all timelines Level 2
git switch <name> Travel to another timeline Level 2
git add <file> Put the file in the basket Level 3
git commit -m "label" Take the photo, with a label Level 3
git diff Show exactly what changed Level 4
git restore <file> Discard unstaged edits to this file Level 4

What branches look like in a real project. Now that you know the commands, this is what they produce in a real project: the history of a real app (Degreez, your TA Ramzy's project), as VS Code's Source Control graph shows it:

  • Each dot is a save point (commit), with its label: feat(hub): …, fix(community): …, docs(owner): …. The labels follow a common habit, type(area): what changed, so anyone can read the history.
  • Each coloured line is a timeline (branch): several pieces of work side by side, none touching the others.
  • "Merge branch … into develop": a finished timeline joins back. Here the main line is called develop; in your project it is main. Merging is Week 2.

The same project on a busier day: about ten timelines side by side. One feature (the brown line) is eight small save points — code, tests and docs, each with its own label — which is what makes one change easy to find and undo later.

Your turn 2b · Git Quest: four levels (19 min, 11:09–11:28)

A real Git repository with a story in it. Each level file tells you what to type and what you should see.

Level You use What you do
1 · Look around git status, git log --oneline Read the history and find the save point whose label starts with KEY.
2 · Travel between timelines git branch, git switch List the timelines and travel to the one the KEY names.
3 · Make your own save point git add, git commit Write your name into a new file and commit it, on that timeline.
4 · Undo a mistake git diff, git restore Back on main, see exactly what a bad edit changed, and undo it.

Start the game:

Step Do this Why
1 Go to your TA1 folder: cd ~/TA1 The quest is built next to the treasure hunt.
2 Download the setup script: curl -fLO https://technionaifluency.github.io/www/exercises/w01/setup_git_quest.sh Same as the treasure hunt: one standalone script that builds the game. The download fails? Appendix B.
3 Build the quest folder: bash ~/TA1/setup_git_quest.sh It makes ~/TA1/git-quest, a real repository with three timelines, and writes the checker ~/TA1/git-quest-check.sh next to it. It does not touch your Git settings. It ends with Git Quest ready! and tells you the next two commands.
4 Go inside the game folder: cd ~/TA1/git-quest Git commands act on the repository you are in.
5 Read the first message: cat START-HERE.txt. Then follow all 4 levels. Levels 1–3 end with NEXT: and the file to read next; Level 4 ends with the checker command.

Steps 1–5, as on the slide, without its # notes:

cd ~/TA1
curl -fLO \
https://technionaifluency.github.io/www/exercises/w01/setup_git_quest.sh

Done when You run bash ~/TA1/git-quest-check.sh and it prints FINAL STATE CHECK PASSED. Then explain to yourself a few of the self-check terms it lists.

The last level tells you to run the checker. On success it prints:

Git Quest check
---------------
[OK] Level 3: explorer.txt is saved in a commit on cave
[OK] Level 4: on main, with no staged, unstaged, or untracked changes
---------------
FINAL STATE CHECK PASSED
This checks the final state, not which commands you typed.

SELF-CHECK: alone or with your neighbor, can you explain these terms?
  - Repository and branch: what are main and cave?
  - Working tree: what do untracked and modified mean?
  - Staging: what does git add prepare?
  - Commit and history: what do git commit and git log show?
  - git status and git diff: what does each one tell you?
  - git restore: which edit did it undo in this game?
Use examples from the quest. If unsure, revisit the relevant level.

Not finished at 11:28? Finish the levels and the checker at home before next week; the checker tells you which level is still open.

The checker checks the final state, not whether you personally used every command. A pass does not prove you did Level 4; the self-check questions are how you find out whether you understood it.

Things that catch people:

  • Author identity unknown at Level 3. Git needs a name and an email for every commit. Level 3 gives the fix, for this game only: git config user.name "Your Name" and git config user.email "your.email@example.com" (your own name and email), then commit again. These two commands affect only this repository.
  • No error, but a long note starting Committer: and Your name and email address were configured automatically (common on a Mac). The commit worked: Git guessed a name and email from your computer. Nothing to fix today; Week 2 sets them properly.
  • WRONG WAY! Go back to the quest. You switched to the timeline called mountain. git switch main, then read the KEY line again.
  • [ ] Level 3: save your name in explorer.txt on cave; add and commit it. Your name is not in a commit on cave yet. Run git switch cave, then Level 3 from Step 1: echo "Your Name" > explorer.txt, git add explorer.txt, git commit -m "Explorer arrived at the cave", then git switch main and run the checker again.
  • [ ] Level 4: return to main and check git status. The map must be restored. You are not on main, or something is still changed. git status says which.
  • Unsaved changes travel with you. Commit your changes before switching; unsaved changes may follow you to the other timeline (Level 2 says so).
  • The git-quest game already exists. Your progress has been kept. You ran the setup twice. To start again, bash ~/TA1/setup_git_quest.sh --reset (it moves the old game into a hidden backup folder in ~/TA1 and prints its name). Run it from ~/TA1, then cd ~/TA1/git-quest again. If you used Appendix B, the script is in your home folder: bash ~/setup_git_quest.sh --reset.
  • The setup stops with an error about -b (added after the session). Your Git is older than 2.28 (git --version says which). The script stops after making the git-quest folder, so running it again only says the game already exists. Update Git (ask a TA for the route on your system), then start clean: bash ~/TA1/setup_git_quest.sh --reset.

Part 3 · How an agent works (22 min)

By the end of this part, you can:

  • Explain what an AI agent is made of, and what the human does.

Watch 3a · The brain, the hands, and the loop (10 min, 11:38–11:48)

The brain and the hands.

  • LLM — the model. It receives inputs and requests tools. Here, the inputs are text.
  • Harness — the hands. A program on your computer. It runs tools for the LLM.
  • LLM + harness = agent — together, in a loop.

Fig. 7The brain and the hands: the LLM is the brain, the harness is the hands, together they make the agent; the human directs and checks

The LLM thinks. The harness acts. The human directs and checks. We learn more about agents in Weeks 2 & 3.

Words you will meet:

Word Meaning
Tool a command the harness can run
Observation the result that goes back to the LLM
Memory the history the harness keeps

The agent loop.

  1. Think — the LLM decides what it needs.
  2. Request — the LLM asks for one tool.
  3. Run — the harness runs the tool.
  4. Report — the result goes back to the LLM.

Then back to Think, again and again. Agents may repeat this many times, by themselves.

Fig. 8The agent loop: Think, the LLM decides what it needs; Request, the LLM asks for one tool; Run, the harness runs the tool; Report, the result goes back to the LLM; then again and again

The human in the loop.

  1. Direct — give the agent a clear task.
  2. Approve — check requests before approving.
  3. Verify — check the result against your goal.
  4. Decide — keep it, or undo it (Git!).

Then back to Direct: stay in the loop. You are responsible for what the agent does.

Fig. 9The human in the loop: around the agent's Think, Request, Run and Report runs the human's ring, Direct, Approve, Verify and Decide; stay in the loop

Your turn 3b · Working with an agent: check yourself (12 min, 11:48–12:00)

Answer each question out loud, or with your neighbour, before you reveal the answer.

Question Answer
The model requests ls. Who runs it? The harness runs the command and returns the file list to the model. The human directs and checks.
What do you check before approving a file change? Read the command. Check which file it changes and whether the action matches your goal.
The agent says "Done". How do you verify? Read the file and compare it with the task. For a tracked file, inspect git diff.
How can Git help undo a mistake? Commit the working version first. For a tracked file, git restore can discard an unstaged edit.

git diff and git restore, in the last two answers, are Level 4 of the Git Quest: that is how you check, and undo, what an agent did to your files.

Your harness: next step.

When What
Now — today Nothing to install. Basic understanding.
Next — before TA session 2 We will send instructions. Install it at home.

Added after the session. The timing has changed: harnesses are installed at home before Week 3, not before TA session 2. The instructions are in the Week 2 handout ("Before Week 3 · Set up your harnesses").

Part 4 · Your project topic (15 min)

By the end of this part, you can:

  • Find the simulator that could compute the answer.
  • Start your proposal today, and finish it at home.

Your project, in three questions.

  1. The problem and goal. What should improve? How will you measure it? What limits matter?
  2. The simulator. A program that computes how a system behaves. You give it inputs; it returns results.
  3. The agent's job. What will the agent decide or change? Why might it need reasoning?

Added after the session: the simulator is the ground. In the lecture and in the rest of the course, the simulator is called the ground: a tested, deterministic program the agent calls. Before you name one, check it against the six criteria on the Project page. As the page states them:

  1. Importable in Python, and exposes a callable API
  2. Free tier or open source
  3. Deterministic
  4. Bounded and fast
  5. Testable
  6. Non-trivial enough to need reasoning, but not so hard the loop cannot progress

The boundary between what the model reasons about and what the ground computes is called the line. Question 3 is your first guess at it. The guess is meant to be wrong; it is corrected in Week 6.

A clear topic, and a vague one.

  • Too vague: "I want to use AI to improve traffic."
  • Clear: "Cars wait too long at one busy junction. I want to find traffic-light timings that reduce the average waiting time."

A clear topic says what changes, and which result improves.

One full example.

  1. The problem. Cars wait too long at a busy junction. We want to reduce their waiting time.
  2. The simulator. A program that simulates traffic at the junction. We set how long each light stays green. It calculates how long cars wait.
  3. The agent's job. Suggest how long each light should stay green. Use the simulator to check whether waiting times improve. Each green light must last at least 10 seconds.

Fig. 11The traffic-junction example: a busy junction where cars wait too long; the agent suggests how long each light stays green, at least 10 seconds; the simulator of the junction returns how long cars wait

No simulation tool is installed or invoked in this example.

Does this task need an LLM?

A fixed search may be enough:

  • Try a fixed set of traffic-light timings.
  • Run the simulator for each option.
  • Choose the option with the shortest waiting time that meets the constraints.

An LLM might also…

  • Turn a written request, such as "give buses priority", into goals and constraints.
  • Use the results to suggest and explain the next experiment.
  • Help adapt the plan when the requirements change.

The for-loop test: remove the LLM. Can a simple search solve the task just as well? A possible role is not enough. We need to test whether the LLM actually helps.

Fig. 12The for-loop test: a fixed search runs the simulator for each of a set of timings and keeps the shortest wait that meets the constraints, against what an LLM might also add; remove the LLM, and can a simple search solve the task just as well?

Your turn 4b · Draft your project proposal (9 min, 12:06–12:15)

Step Do this Why
1 Make a project folder, start Git: mkdir -p ~/my-project/docs, then cd ~/my-project, then git init -b main Your project gets its own repository from day one, with main as its first timeline. docs/ is where its written documents live.
2 Download the proposal template: curl -fL -o docs/project-proposal.md https://technionaifluency.github.io/www/exercises/w01/project-proposal.md -o names the saved file: the template lands at docs/project-proposal.md. Download it once: a second download replaces your answers. The download fails? Appendix B, last part.
3 Write each answer in place of its <!-- … --> line; save: code ~/my-project/docs/project-proposal.md Opens the file in VS Code. Write your answers in place of each <!-- Write your … here. --> comment: four of them, including the last one, <!-- Write your explanation here. -->.
4 Count the placeholders left: grep -c '<!--' docs/project-proposal.md (added after the session) Each answered section is one placeholder comment fewer. Delete each comment as you replace it with your answer. The fresh template prints 4.

Steps 1–3, as on the slide, without its # notes:

mkdir -p ~/my-project/docs
cd ~/my-project
git init -b main
curl -fL -o docs/project-proposal.md \
https://technionaifluency.github.io/www/exercises/w01/project-proposal.md
code ~/my-project/docs/project-proposal.md

Done when (added after the session) grep -c '<!--' docs/project-proposal.md prints less than 4 today: at least one section is answered. Before your homework commit it must print 0. Week 2 uses the same check.

What the template asks, section by section (from project-proposal.md; changed after the session: it no longer asks for your name or the date, because the repository stays anonymous and GitHub records who posted it and when):

Section What to write
1. The problem and goal The problem and why it matters; what you want to improve, how you will measure improvement, and which limits or requirements must be respected.
2. The simulator A program or model that could simulate your system: its inputs and results, whether it runs on your computer with inputs in a text file (such as JSON or YAML). Not chosen yet? Name an option to explore and what you need to check.
3. The agent's role What the agent will decide or change, and how it uses the simulator's results to choose its next action; the variables and their ranges, if known; the for-loop question; one question you still need to answer.
Explain your project to someone outside your field One or two short paragraphs in everyday language, connecting all three parts. Do not simply copy your answers above.

Things that catch people:

  • code: command not found. VS Code is recommended, not required. Open the file in any text editor, for example nano ~/my-project/docs/project-proposal.md. In nano, type your answers, press Ctrl+O then Enter to save, and Ctrl+X to exit. On a Mac with VS Code installed: open it, press Cmd+Shift+P, run Shell Command: Install 'code' command in PATH, then open a new Terminal.
  • Writing "use AI to improve X". That is the vague topic above. Say what changes, and which result improves.
  • No simulator yet. The template allows a candidate: name one option and what you still need to check.

Commit and close (5 min)

Your turn Save your proposal in Git (12:15)

Step Do this Why
1 Go to your project folder: cd ~/my-project Git commands act on the repository you are in.
2 Save your proposal in Git: git add docs/project-proposal.md, then git commit -m "Add project proposal" Put the file in the basket, then take the photo, with a label: your first save point.
3 Check your commit and status: git log --oneline, then git status The log shows your commit; the status shows nothing left to save. 
cd ~/my-project
git add docs/project-proposal.md
git commit -m "Add project proposal"
git log --oneline
git status

Done when Your commit is in the history, and the working tree is clean.

git log --oneline shows one line ending in Add project proposal; git status ends with nothing to commit, working tree clean.

Today: your proposal is saved in Git on your computer. Next week: we will learn GitHub and upload your proposal there. The course staff will review and grade it on GitHub.

Things that catch people:

  • Author identity unknown. The Git Quest set your name and email inside the game's repository only, so ~/my-project does not have them. Run the same two git config commands from Level 3 inside ~/my-project, then commit again.

Added after the session. From Week 2, every session ends with a commit and one line in docs/disclosure.md. The Week 2 handout shows how.

Fast finishers (added after the session): a timeline you can throw away.

The lecture's reason for branches: an agent that edits your files should do it somewhere you can discard. Try it by hand, after your commit, inside ~/my-project.

First run git status. It must say nothing to commit, working tree clean. If it does not, commit your proposal first: git restore below throws away every uncommitted change to the file, not only the risky line.

git switch -c try
echo "a risky idea" >> docs/project-proposal.md
git diff
git restore docs/project-proposal.md
git switch main
git branch -d try

Line by line: a new timeline, starting at your commit; a risky edit; exactly what changed; undo it; back to main; delete the timeline.

git status ends with nothing to commit, working tree clean, and git branch lists only main.

What we did: you now have

  • A terminal you can use without fear.
  • Saved versions, and practice switching branches.
  • The agent loop, and your four jobs in it.
  • Start your project topic.

Appendix A · The treasure hunt route

The whole route, for when the hints are not enough. Try the hints in Part 1 first: finding the way is the exercise.

Show the full route

Start in ~/TA1/treasure (ls shows README.txt, desert, forest, mountain, start).

Move Do this What the clue says
1 cd start, then cat clue1.txt The next clue is in forest, next to the folder you are in: go up one level with cd ...
2 cd .., then cd forest, then cat clue2.txt Three folders here; only one has a name about a secret. (tree and river are dead ends; so is desert.)
3 cd cave-of-secrets, then cat clue3.txt The key is in mountain, two levels above this cave: cd ../...
4 cd ../.., then cd mountain, then cat clue4.txt Go up to treasure, make a folder called done, and move golden_key.txt into it.
5 cd .., then mkdir done, then mv mountain/golden_key.txt done/ The key is now in done. Check with the two ls lines in Part 1.
6 Bonus: cd mountain, then ls -a, then cat .bonus.txt Hidden files start with a dot. Git keeps its settings in hidden files and folders too, such as .git.

Backup Appendix B · If the download fails

Use this only if the curl step fails. It works for both games: replace SCRIPT below with setup_treasure.sh or setup_git_quest.sh. Run only the commands for the game you are in.

Step Do this Why
1 Download the file in your browser: open the course website's Exercises page, find W01, and save setup_treasure.sh or setup_git_quest.sh (right-click the link, then Save link as…) The script goes to your Downloads folder.
2 Copy it to your home folder: the Windows or the Mac command below On Windows, Ubuntu sees your Downloads folder under /mnt/c/Users/NAME/; the copy brings the script into your home folder, ~.
3 Check that it is there: ls ~ You should see the script's name.
4 Then go on with the game. Skip the curl step: run bash ~/SCRIPT instead of bash ~/TA1/SCRIPT The script builds the game in ~/TA1 wherever it is run from.

cp ~/Downloads/setup_treasure.sh ~/

Appendix C · Command cheat sheet

Both tables on one page, to print or keep open beside your terminal.

The terminal: twelve commands, three purposes.

Look around Change things Read and get
Where am I, what is here? Make, copy, move, delete. Read, write, download, run.
pwd — Where am I? mkdir <name> — Make a folder cat <file> — Show what is inside
ls — What is in this folder? cp a b — Copy a file echo "hi" > file — Write text into a file
cd <folder> — Go into a folder mv a b — Move or rename a file curl -fLO URL — Download a file
cd .. — Go up one folder rm file — Delete without a recycle bin bash script.sh — Run a script

~ is your home folder, .. the folder one level above. > replaces a file's contents; >> adds at the end.

Git, in plain words.

Look Save Travel Undo
git status — What does Git see right now? git add <file> — Put the file in the basket git branch — Show all timelines git diff — Show exactly what changed
git log --oneline — Show commits on this branch git commit -m "label" — Take the photo, with a label git switch <name> — Travel to another timeline git restore <file> — Discard unstaged edits to this file

git init creates a repository here. The LLM thinks. The harness acts. The human directs and checks.
